blocks.text: An intensive care patient has a chest radiograph labelled 'AP supine' and the heart looks enormous. The trainee writes 'cardiomegaly, heart failure'. The consultant radiologist crosses it out. The same heart on an erect PA film in the same patient would look normal. A radiograph is a flattened shadow, and reading it safely starts with how it was taken.

blocks.markdown: **Always start with the film, not the finding.** Before looking for disease, confirm the *patient identity* and date, the *projection* (PA erect, AP erect or AP supine), and the *technical quality*: **rotation** (the medial ends of the clavicles equidistant from the spinous processes), **inspiration** (generally about five to six anterior ribs, or nine to ten posterior ribs, above the diaphragm), and **penetration** (vertebral bodies just visible behind the heart). Then follow the same sequence on every film so that a dramatic finding does not distract from a quiet one: this is the principle of a **systematic approach**. One widely taught order for the chest is A for airway, B for breathing, C for circulation, D for diaphragm and E for everything else.

headers: What to check on a chest radiograph
rows: Airway
Trachea midline, carina and main bronchi
Tracheal deviation by mass or tension pneumothorax
Breathing
Lung fields compared side to side, pleura, fissures
Consolidation, collapse, pneumothorax, effusion, nodules
Circulation
Heart size and borders, mediastinal contour, hila
Cardiomegaly, widened mediastinum, hilar enlargement
Diaphragm
Both hemidiaphragms, costophrenic angles, gas beneath
Blunted angle (effusion), raised diaphragm, free gas
Everything else
Bones, soft tissue, lines and tubes, upper abdomen, edges of the film
Rib fracture, lytic lesion, misplaced line, surgical emphysema
blocks.caption: A systematic sequence for reading a chest radiograph.

blocks.latex: \mathrm{CTR}=\frac{\text{maximum transverse cardiac diameter}}{\text{maximum internal thoracic diameter}}
blocks.caption: The cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) is measured on a PA erect film; a value above about 0.5 suggests cardiomegaly. On AP films the heart is magnified, so the ratio overestimates heart size.

blocks.title: Calculating the cardiothoracic ratio
blocks.prompt: On a PA erect chest radiograph in a 60-year-old man, the maximum transverse cardiac diameter is 15.0 cm and the maximum internal thoracic diameter is 32.0 cm. Calculate and interpret the cardiothoracic ratio.

steps.text: Compare with the threshold. A CTR above about 0.5 on a PA erect film suggests an enlarged heart, so 0.47 is within the usual limit.

Qualify. The ratio is only valid for a PA film with a good inspiration; an AP film would exaggerate heart size, and a normal ratio does not exclude heart disease such as a small pericardial effusion or ventricular hypertrophy.

blocks.answer: The CTR is 0.47, within the usual limit on a PA erect film.

blocks.markdown: **The abdominal radiograph** is read in the same disciplined way: confirm the patient and projection, then look at *bowel gas* (distribution and calibre), *free gas* (under the diaphragm on an erect chest film or outlining the bowel wall), *soft tissue outlines* (liver, spleen, kidneys, psoas margins), *calcification* (renal tract stones, vascular calcification, gallstones, pancreatic calcification), *bones* (spine, pelvis, hips) and finally *tubes, lines, surgical clips and foreign bodies*. A useful mnemonic is to check the 'gas, stones, soft tissue and bones'. The abdominal film has limited sensitivity and is used mainly for suspected obstruction, toxic megacolon and foreign bodies; CT is generally used for acute abdominal pain.

**Three common chest findings.** *Pneumonia* appears as airspace **consolidation**, a fluffy or homogeneous opacity with **air bronchograms** (dark branching bronchi within white lung). The **silhouette sign** localises it: loss of the right heart border indicates the right middle lobe, loss of the left heart border the lingula, and loss of the hemidiaphragm outline a lower lobe. *Pulmonary oedema from heart failure* shows upper lobe vessel diversion, **Kerley B lines** (short horizontal lines at the lung periphery from thickened interlobular septa), peribronchial cuffing, perihilar 'bat's wing' alveolar opacity, cardiomegaly on a PA film and pleural effusions. *Pneumothorax* shows a thin **visceral pleural line** with absent lung markings beyond it; on a supine film, air collects anteriorly and may produce a deep, lucent costophrenic sulcus. Tension pneumothorax, with mediastinal shift away from the lesion, is a clinical diagnosis that needs immediate treatment without waiting for imaging.

rows: Pneumonia
Consolidation, air bronchograms, silhouette sign, sometimes small effusion
May lag behind symptoms; a normal early film does not exclude pneumonia
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, bat's wing opacity, cardiomegaly, effusions
AP films overestimate heart size; consolidation can mimic oedema
Pneumothorax
Visceral pleural line, absent lung markings peripherally, collapse of lung edge
A skin fold or clothing line can mimic a pleural line, but lung markings continue beyond it
Pleural effusion
Meniscus sign, blunted costophrenic angle; layering posteriorly on supine film
Small effusions are missed on supine films
blocks.caption: Key features of common chest conditions.

blocks.title: Interpreting a consolidation
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old man has 3 days of fever and a productive cough. The PA erect chest radiograph shows a hazy airspace opacity in the right mid zone with air bronchograms. The right heart border is obscured, the right hemidiaphragm is clear and the costophrenic angles are sharp. Interpret the findings.

steps.text: Check technique. The film is PA erect, so heart size and effusions are reliably assessed.
Characterise the opacity. A fluffy airspace opacity with air bronchograms is consolidation, in which air-filled bronchi are outlined by fluid-filled alveoli.

Localise with the silhouette sign. Loss of the right heart border means the opacity touches that border, which lies against the right middle lobe, whereas a clear diaphragm indicates the lower lobe is spared.

Integrate and report. Right middle lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia in this febrile patient, with no effusion. Follow-up imaging in suitable patients, such as older smokers, may be recommended to confirm resolution and exclude an underlying lesion.

blocks.answer: Right middle lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia, with no effusion, correlated with the clinical picture.

blocks.markdown: **Presenting an image with its limits.** Present in a fixed order: *identify* (patient, date, type of film and projection), *comment on technique and limitations* (rotation, inspiration, penetration, projection), *describe the findings* using anatomical words rather than a diagnosis, give an *impression* with a ranked differential, and state *what to do next*. Use language that matches your confidence: 'consistent with', 'suggestive of' and 'cannot be excluded' are different strengths. Name what the image cannot answer: a radiograph is a two-dimensional projection, small lesions can be hidden behind the heart, ribs or diaphragm, and a normal film does not exclude disease. Compare with previous films whenever possible and always correlate with the patient.

blocks.caption: Likelihood ratio (LR) formulation of Bayes' theorem. A positive result with a high positive LR raises the probability of disease, but the pre-test probability matters.

blocks.title: Updating the probability of pneumonia after a film
blocks.prompt: Before imaging, a clinician judges the probability of pneumonia in a febrile, coughing patient to be 20%. For teaching, assume a chest radiograph showing consolidation has a positive likelihood ratio of 6. What is the probability after the film?

steps.text: Convert the pre-test probability to odds. Odds = 0.20 / (1 - 0.20) = 0.25.
Multiply by the likelihood ratio. Post-test odds = 0.25 x 6 = 1.5.
Convert back to probability. p = 1.5 / (1 + 1.5) = 0.60, or 60%.

Interpret and state limits. A positive film raises the probability from 20% to 60%, which is meaningful but not certain; the figure depends on the assumed likelihood ratio and the pre-test estimate, which is why the report states uncertainty and the clinician combines it with the clinical picture.

blocks.answer: The post-test probability is 60%, increased but not certain, so the report should state its confidence and limits.

blocks.title: Say what you see, then what it means, then what you do not know
blocks.text: In an examination or on the ward, describe findings before naming a diagnosis, give a short differential in order of likelihood, state the limits (such as 'AP supine film, cannot assess heart size reliably') and suggest the next step, for example repeat erect film, comparison with old films, ultrasound or CT.

points: Check patient, projection and technical quality, then follow the same sequence every time (airway, breathing, circulation, diaphragm, everything else for the chest; gas, stones, soft tissue and bones for the abdomen).
Cardiothoracic ratio above about 0.5 on a PA erect film suggests cardiomegaly; AP films exaggerate heart size.

Pneumonia shows consolidation and air bronchograms with silhouette sign; heart failure shows upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, bat's wing opacity and effusions; pneumothorax shows a visceral pleural line with absent markings, and tension is a clinical emergency.
Present findings with identification, technique, description, impression, differential and next steps, using language that reflects uncertainty and the limits of a two-dimensional film.

questions.stem: Why is the cardiothoracic ratio unreliable on an AP supine chest radiograph taken at the bedside?

options.text: The film cannot show the heart at all
Ribs are not visible on AP films
Magnification and the supine position make the heart look larger than it is
AP films always show lower inspiration than PA films

questions.correctOptionText: Magnification and the supine position make the heart look larger than it is

distractorRationale.a: The heart is visible on AP films.
distractorRationale.b: Ribs are visible on both projections.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the heart is farther from the detector and the supine position redistributes blood, so it appears larger.
distractorRationale.d: Inspiration depends on the patient's effort, not on projection.

questions.explanation: On an AP film the heart is anterior and farther from the detector, so it is magnified, and a supine position can enlarge the mediastinum. The cardiothoracic ratio should therefore be quoted only for PA erect films.

questions.stem: A chest radiograph shows an airspace opacity that obscures the left heart border but leaves the left hemidiaphragm outline sharp. Which lung segment is most likely involved?

options.text: The lingula of the left upper lobe

questions.correctOptionText: The lingula of the left upper lobe

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the lingula abuts the left heart border, so disease there erases that border while the diaphragm remains clear.
distractorRationale.b: A lower lobe opacity would blur the diaphragm outline rather than the heart border.
distractorRationale.c: The right middle lobe abuts the right heart border.
distractorRationale.d: The right lower lobe abuts the right hemidiaphragm.

questions.explanation: The silhouette sign says that an opacity in contact with a border of the same density will obliterate that border. The lingula lies against the left heart border and the lower lobe against the diaphragm, so the pattern localises the opacity.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has orthopnoea and ankle swelling. Her PA erect chest film shows short horizontal lines at the periphery of the lower zones, upper lobe vessel enlargement and small bilateral effusions. What are the peripheral horizontal lines?

options.text: Kerley B lines from thickened interlobular septa

questions.correctOptionText: Kerley B lines from thickened interlobular septa

distractorRationale.a: Air bronchograms are dark branching bronchi within opacity.
distractorRationale.b: A visceral pleural line is a thin edge of lung with absent markings beyond it.
distractorRationale.c: Rib notching is a rib abnormality, not peripheral lung lines.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: they reflect interstitial fluid in the septa and signal pulmonary oedema.

questions.explanation: Kerley B lines are short, horizontal, peripheral lines from interstitial oedema and, together with upper lobe diversion and effusions, support heart failure. Consolidation and pneumothorax have different signs.

questions.stem: A tall, thin 22-year-old man has sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain. The PA erect film shows a thin line about 2 cm from the chest wall at the right apex, with no lung markings lateral to it. What is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Normal film with a skin fold

distractorRationale.a: Consolidation is a dense opacity, not a line with lucent space beyond.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it indicates air in the pleural space.
distractorRationale.c: Heart failure shows central opacities and Kerley B lines.
distractorRationale.d: A skin fold usually lets lung markings continue beyond the line.

questions.explanation: The thin line is the edge of the collapsed lung, and the absence of vessels peripheral to it shows air in the pleural space. This differs from a skin fold, where lung markings continue beyond the edge.

questions.stem: A film shows a left lower zone opacity on an AP supine film in a ventilated patient. Which wording best conveys appropriate diagnostic uncertainty?

options.text: Left lower lobe pneumonia, antibiotics needed
Left lower zone opacity on an AP supine film, which may represent consolidation, collapse or an effusion; compare with previous films and consider ultrasound or CT

questions.correctOptionText: Left lower zone opacity on an AP supine film, which may represent consolidation, collapse or an effusion; compare with previous films and consider ultrasound or CT

distractorRationale.a: It commits to a diagnosis that the film cannot establish.
distractorRationale.b: On a supine film effusions layer and may look like haziness; certainty is not possible.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it describes the finding, names the limits of the film, lists a differential and proposes next steps.

questions.explanation: A good report states the technical limitation, offers a ranked differential and advises how to resolve the uncertainty. Overconfident wording is unsafe when a supine film cannot distinguish consolidation, collapse and effusion.

questions.stem: On a PA erect chest radiograph the maximum transverse cardiac diameter is 17.5 cm and the maximum internal thoracic diameter is 31.0 cm. Calculate the cardiothoracic ratio to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: CTR = 17.5 / 31.0 = 0.565, which rounds to 0.56. A value above about 0.5 on a PA erect film suggests cardiomegaly, which requires clinical correlation and may need echocardiography.

questions.stem: Before the chest radiograph a clinician estimates a 25% probability of pneumonia. Assume that a film showing consolidation has a positive likelihood ratio of 6. Calculate the post-test probability as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Pre-test odds = 0.25 / 0.75 = 0.333; post-test odds = 0.333 x 6 = 2.0; probability = 2.0 / (1 + 2.0) = 0.667, or 66.7%. The film raises the probability substantially but not to certainty, so the report should express this uncertainty.

questions.stem: Describe a systematic approach to reading a chest radiograph and an abdominal radiograph, including how you check technical quality first.
markingGuide: Identify patient, date and projection (PA, AP, erect, supine)
Chest: airway, breathing, circulation, diaphragm, everything else
Abdomen: gas pattern and calibre, free gas, soft tissue, calcification, bones, lines and tubes
Review areas easily missed such as lung apices, behind the heart and below the diaphragm
Compare with previous films and correlate clinically
questions.explanation: A fixed sequence prevents satisfaction of search, in which one obvious finding distracts from others. Checking technique first prevents misinterpreting artefact, such as magnification or rotation, as disease.

questions.stem: Compare the radiographic features of pneumonia, cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and pneumothorax, and state one important pitfall for each.
markingGuide: Pneumonia: consolidation, air bronchograms, silhouette sign; may lag behind symptoms
Pulmonary oedema: upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, bat's wing opacity, cardiomegaly, effusions; AP films overestimate heart size
Pneumothorax: visceral pleural line, absent lung markings beyond; skin folds can mimic; supine films show deep sulcus sign
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis with immediate treatment
Pneumonia versus oedema can overlap and need clinical correlation
questions.explanation: Each condition has a characteristic distribution and accompanying signs, and the pitfalls often depend on technique and timing. Using the full set of signs rather than one avoids false conclusions.

questions.stem: You are presenting a bedside chest radiograph from a ventilated patient to your consultant. Outline how to structure the presentation and how to express the limits of the image and your uncertainty.
markingGuide: Identify patient, date, projection (AP supine) and quality
Describe findings before naming diagnoses, using anatomical terms
Use calibrated language such as consistent with, suggestive of, cannot exclude
Name limitations: AP supine magnification, small effusions missed, overlying structures, normal does not exclude disease
Suggest next steps: repeat film, comparison, ultrasound or CT
questions.explanation: A structured presentation separates observation from interpretation and communicates confidence honestly. Acknowledging limits is part of safe practice because decisions may rest on the report.
